samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers give a ranked, well-reasoned audit that covers the same ground: cut the stagger, the slide and the bounce; add save and lab-result feedback; tone down the shake; keep the refill checkmark. B states a few usage claims as fact without data, such as tab switches being the most frequent action, where A hedges its one assumption about older patients. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers give a sound ranked audit and cover the same ground: cut the stagger, the slow tab slide and the logo bounce; add save and lab-result feedback; keep the refill checkmark. pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers cover the same core moves: cutting the stagger, tab slide and bounce; adding save and lab-result feedback; toning down the shake; and keeping the refill checkmark. B is a little longer and more spec-heavy, but the extra detail (interruptible tabs, the WCAG three-flash concern, keeping opacity under reduced motion) earns its place. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers cover the same ground well: cutting the stagger, the tab slide and the logo bounce, adding save and lab-result feedback, keeping the refill checkmark, and softening the error shake with text. pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers cover the rubric well: each cuts the slide, the stagger and the bounce for repeated use, adds signals for the form save and lab results, keeps the refill checkmark with checks, and tones down the shake with text and reduced-motion handling. samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Answer B is stronger on keeping the layout stable, with tabular figures, fixed-width score cells and in-place status changes. It also handles several changes at once by having them fade together and avoiding a burst of flashing when someone returns. However, its markers stay until the change has been seen, which partly conflicts with the rubric's warning against cues that persist until dismissed. Answer A gives sensible long fades with concrete timings and good off-screen cues, but it never says what happens when many cells change in one refresh, and its '+4' deltas could cause layout shift. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers update cells in place, use two tiers so wickets stand out, add a polite live region and keep the layout stable. A is stronger because it gives precise timing (about 150 ms in, about 1.5 s fade), uses tabular figures and fixed-width score cells to prevent layout shift, and has updates that land together fade in step. A loses some credit because its 'seen' markers stay until the user hovers, taps or scrolls to the match. B's 30–60 s highlights are not short-lived, and it doesn't really deal with many cells changing in one refresh.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): B says outright that it diffs each poll and touches only the cells that changed. It gives precise timings, including a summary table, with no loops or persistent cues, and it adds thoughtful details such as reserving space for the W chip and leaving finished matches in place. A covers similar ground and handles the flood of changes on first load or a returning tab better, but its timings are looser and its wicket line stays until the next event. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): A is better overall. It gives more precise timing (2.5 s ease-out fade, about 60 s for the 'updated' dot, about 2 min for the wicket chip), reserves space for the W chip so nothing shifts, and announces changes through one polite live region. B handles multiple changes better: it avoids a burst of animation on first load or when a hidden tab comes back. But B's wicket line stays until the next event, it doesn't say how to fit that line in without shifting the layout, and it only announces changes to screen readers for followed matches.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Answer A gives a tighter, more concrete spec. It highlights only the changed cell, gives exact durations (1.5 s, 2 s, a 60 s marker and a 300 ms fade-out), bans loops and flashing, and uses tabular numerals to prevent layout shift. Answer B has good ideas, such as tiered importance, starred matches and a summary after the tab becomes visible again, but its timings are looser and it applies the highlight to the whole card for wickets. Both handle reduced motion and screen-reader announcements well and batch simultaneous changes reasonably. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers recommend in-place updates, keeping the layout still, an off-screen pill, a tab-title marker and polite live regions. B is more precise: it uses tabular-nums so the digits can't shift the layout, bans looping pulses and repeated flashing outright, gives a clear timing table, says what to do when a new update arrives mid-fade, and spells out how reduced motion should behave. A adds useful ideas, such as a catch-up summary when the tab becomes visible again and starring favourite matches, but it highlights the whole card for wickets and gives less exact rules on motion and layout.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers keep stale content dimmed, use a 300ms threshold with a minimum display time, and specify a clear failure banner with Retry, kept separate from the zero-results state. A is very precise on timing and handles a partial failure (list loads, pins fail), but on the map the only loading signal is dimmed pins, so the signal near the map is weaker. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers keep stale results visible, wait 300ms before showing anything, and handle failure well, with a plain-language banner, a Retry button and a warning mark on the changed chip. It also covers partial failure, a 'Still working…' state with Cancel, and exact timing specs. A localizes loading a little better with a dedicated map pill, while B deliberately keeps one indicator and only dims the pins.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers keep old content visible, wait about 300 ms before showing a loading cue, and handle failure well with an inline banner and Retry. B is stronger on map-local cues and retry logic, but it swaps the old results for skeletons after 1.5 s, which undercuts both keeping previous results visible and avoiding layout shift. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers keep stale content visible, put cues near what's changing, use a roughly 300ms threshold and handle failure well with an inline banner and Retry. pass 1 (A=with, B=without): A keeps the old results and pins visible for the whole wait. But after 1 s, B replaces the list with skeletons, which breaks its own rule of keeping the old results visible. A's weak point is that it deliberately shows nothing on the map while loading. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): B is the more internally consistent design.
